<div class='catholicadnet-728x90' id='summa-728x90-top' style='display: flex; height: 100px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; '></div>

<h1>Question 94. The natural law</h1>

<ol><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article1"> What is the natural law?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article2"> What are the precepts of the natural law?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article3"> Are all acts of virtue prescribed by the natural law?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article4"> Is the natural law the same in all?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article5"> Is it changeable?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2094.htm#article6"> Can it be abolished from the heart of man?</a> </li></ol>

<h2 id="article1">Article 1. Whether the natural law is a habit?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>. Because, as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. ii, 5), "there are three things in the <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a>: power, <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>, and passion." But the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not one of the <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul's</a> powers: nor is it one of the <a href="../cathen/11534a.htm">passions</a>; as we may see by going through them one by one. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/02330b.htm">Basil</a> [Damascene, De Fide Orth. iv, 22 says that the <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a> or <a href="../cathen/14384a.htm">"synderesis"</a> is the "<a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of our <a href="../cathen/10321a.htm">mind</a>"; which can only apply to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. But the <a href="../cathen/14384a.htm">"synderesis"</a> is a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>, as was shown in the <a href="../summa/1079.htm#article12">I:79:12</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> abides in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> always, as will be shown further on (<a href="#article6">Article 6</a>). But <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man's</a> reason, which the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> regards, does not always think about the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not an act, but a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Bono Conjug. xxi) that "a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> is that whereby something is done when <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a>." But such is not the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>: since it is in infants and in the damned who cannot act by it. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> A thing may be called a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> in two ways. First, properly and <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">essentially</a>: and thus the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>. For it has been stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">I-II:90:1 ad 2</a>) that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is something appointed by reason, just as a proposition is a work of reason. Now that which a man does is not the same as that whereby he does it: for he makes a becoming speech by the <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> of grammar. Since then a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> is that by which we act, a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> cannot be a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> properly and <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">essentially</a>.</p>



<p>Secondly, the term <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> may be applied to that which we hold by a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>: thus <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> may mean that which we hold by <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>. And accordingly, since the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> are sometimes considered by reason actually, while sometimes they are in the reason only <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habitually</a>, in this way the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> may be called a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>. Thus, in speculative matters, the indemonstrable principles are not the <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> itself whereby we hold those principles, but are the principles the <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> of which we possess.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> proposes there to discover the genus of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>; and since it is evident that <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> is a principle of action, he mentions only those things which are principles of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>, viz. powers, <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habits</a> and <a href="../cathen/11534a.htm">passions</a>. But there are other things in the <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a> besides these three: there are acts; thus "to will" is in the one that wills; again, things <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> are in the knower; moreover its own <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> properties are in the <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a>, such as <a href="../cathen/07687a.htm">immortality</a> and the like.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> "Synderesis" is said to be the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of our <a href="../cathen/10321a.htm">mind</a>, because it is a <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> containing the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, which are the first principles of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> This argument proves that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is held <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habitually</a>; and this is granted.</p>

<p>To the argument advanced in the contrary sense we reply that sometimes a man is unable to make use of that which is in him <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habitually</a>, on account of some impediment: thus, on account of sleep, a man is unable to use the <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> of science. In like manner, through the deficiency of his age, a child cannot use the <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> of understanding of principles, or the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, which is in him <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habitually</a>.</p>

<h2 id="article2">Article 2. Whether the natural law contains several precepts, or only one?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> contains, not several precepts, but one only. For <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is a kind of precept, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2092.htm#article2">I-II:92:2</a>). If therefore there were many precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, it would follow that there are also many <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> laws.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is consequent to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>. But <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, as a whole, is one; though, as to its parts, it is manifold. Therefore, either there is but one precept of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, on account of the unity of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> as a whole; or there are many, by reason of the number of parts of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>. The result would be that even things relating to the inclination of the <a href="../cathen/04208a.htm">concupiscible</a> faculty belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is something pertaining to reason, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">I-II:90:1</a>). Now reason is but one in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>. Therefore there is only one precept of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> stand in relation to practical matters, as the first principles to matters of demonstration. But there are several first indemonstrable principles. Therefore there are also several precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2091.htm#article3">I-II:91:3</a>), the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> are to the practical reason, what the first principles of demonstrations are to the speculative reason; because both are self-evident principles. Now a thing is said to be self-evident in two ways: first, in itself; secondly, in relation to us. Any proposition is said to be self-evident in itself, if its predicate is contained in the notion of the subject: although, to one who <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knows</a> not the definition of the subject, it happens that such a proposition is not self-evident. For instance, this proposition, "Man is a rational being," is, in its very <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, self-evident, since who says "<a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>," says "a rational being": and yet to one who <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knows</a> not what a man is, this proposition is not self-evident. Hence it is that, as <a href="../cathen/02610b.htm">Boethius</a> says (De Hebdom.), certain axioms or propositions are universally self-evident to all; and such are those propositions whose terms are <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all, as, "Every whole is greater than its part," and, "Things equal to one and the same are equal to one another." But some propositions are self-evident only to the wise, who understand the meaning of the terms of such propositions: thus to one who understands that an <a href="../cathen/01476d.htm">angel</a> is not a body, it is self-evident that an <a href="../cathen/01476d.htm">angel</a> is not circumscriptively in a place: but this is not evident to the unlearned, for they cannot grasp it.</p>

<p>Now a certain order is to be found in those things that are apprehended universally. For that which, before aught else, falls under apprehension, is "being," the notion of which is included in all things whatsoever a man apprehends. Wherefore the first indemonstrable principle is that "the same thing cannot be affirmed and denied at the same time," which is based on the notion of "being" and "not-being": and on this principle all others are based, as is stated in Metaph. iv, text. 9. Now as "being" is the first thing that falls under the apprehension simply, so "<a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>" is the first thing that falls under the apprehension of the practical reason, which is directed to action: since every agent acts for an end under the aspect of <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. Consequently the first principle of practical reason is one founded on the notion of <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, viz. that "<a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> is that which all things seek after." Hence this is the first precept of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, that "<a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> is to be done and pursued, and <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> is to be avoided." All other precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> are based upon this: so that whatever the practical reason <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> apprehends as <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man's</a> <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> (or <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>) belongs to the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> as something to be done or avoided.</p>

<p>Since, however, <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> has the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of an end, and <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>, the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of a contrary, hence it is that all those things to which <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> has a <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> inclination, are <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> apprehended by reason as being <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, and consequently as objects of pursuit, and their contraries as <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>, and objects of avoidance. Wherefore according to the order of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> inclinations, is the order of the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. Because in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> there is first of all an inclination to <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> in accordance with the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> which he has in common with all <a href="../cathen/14322c.htm">substances</a>: inasmuch as every <a href="../cathen/14322c.htm">substance</a> seeks the preservation of its own being, according to its <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>: and by reason of this inclination, whatever is a means of preserving <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> life, and of warding off its obstacles, belongs to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. Secondly, there is in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> an inclination to things that pertain to him more specially, according to that <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> which he has in common with other animals: and in virtue of this inclination, those things are said to belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, "which <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> has taught to all animals" [Pandect. Just. I, tit. i], such as sexual intercourse, education of offspring and so forth. Thirdly, there is in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> an inclination to <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, according to the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of his <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>, which <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> is proper to him: thus <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> has a <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> inclination to <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">know</a> the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> about <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, and to live in society: and in this respect, whatever pertains to this inclination belongs to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>; for instance, to shun <a href="../cathen/07648a.htm">ignorance</a>, to avoid offending those among whom one has to live, and other such things regarding the above inclination.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> All these precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> have the character of one <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, inasmuch as they flow from one first precept.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> All the inclinations of any parts whatsoever of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, e.g. of the <a href="../cathen/04208a.htm">concupiscible</a> and irascible parts, in so far as they are ruled by reason, belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, and are reduced to one first precept, as stated above: so that the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> are many in themselves, but are based on one common foundation.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> Although reason is one in itself, yet it directs all things regarding <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>; so that whatever can be ruled by reason, is contained under the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of reason.</p>

<h2 id="article3">Article 3. Whether all acts of virtue are prescribed by the natural law?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that not all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. Because, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article2">I-II:90:2</a>) it is <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">essential</a> to a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that it be ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. But some acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are ordained to the private <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of the <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>, as is evident especially in regards to acts of <a href="../cathen/14481a.htm">temperance</a>. Therefore not all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are the subject of <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, every <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sin</a> is opposed to some <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> act. If therefore all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, it seems to follow that all <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a> are against <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>: whereas this applies to certain special <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, those things which are according to <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> are common to all. But acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are not common to all: since a thing is <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> in one, and <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vicious</a> in another. Therefore not all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/08459b.htm">Damascene</a> says (De Fide Orth. iii, 4) that "<a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a> are <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a>." Therefore <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> acts also are a subject of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> We may speak of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> acts in two ways: first, under the aspect of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>; secondly, as such and such acts considered in their proper <a href="../cathen/14210a.htm">species</a>. If then we speak of acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, considered as <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>, thus all <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> acts belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. For it has been stated (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>) that to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> belongs everything to which a man is inclined according to his <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>. Now each thing is inclined <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> to an operation that is suitable to it according to its <a href="../cathen/06137b.htm">form</a>: thus fire is inclined to give heat. Wherefore, since the rational <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a> is the proper form of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, there is in every <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> a <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> inclination to act according to reason: and this is to act according to <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. Consequently, considered thus, all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>: since each one's reason <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> dictates to him to act virtuously. But if we speak of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> acts, considered in themselves, i.e. in their proper <a href="../cathen/14210a.htm">species</a>, thus not all <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> acts are prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>: for many things are done virtuously, to which <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> does not incline at first; but which, through the inquiry of <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>, have been found by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> to be conducive to well-living.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Temperance is about the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> <a href="../cathen/04208a.htm">concupiscences</a> of food, drink and sexual matters, which are indeed ordained to the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, just as other matters of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> are ordained to the moral common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> By <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> we may mean either that which is proper to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>&#8212;and in this sense all <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a>, as being against reason, are also against <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, as <a href="../cathen/08459b.htm">Damascene</a> states (De Fide Orth. ii, 30): or we may mean that <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> which is common to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> and other animals; and in this sense, certain special <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a> are said to be against <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>; thus contrary to sexual intercourse, which is <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> to all animals, is unisexual <a href="../cathen/09438a.htm">lust</a>, which has received the special name of the unnatural crime.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> This argument considers acts in themselves. For it is owing to the various <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, that certain acts are <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> for some, as being proportionate and becoming to them, while they are <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vicious</a> for others, as being out of proportion to them.</p>

<h2 id="article4">Article 4. Whether the natural law is the same in all men?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not the same in all. For it is stated in the Decretals (Dist. i) that "the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is that which is contained in the <a href="../cathen/10582c.htm">Law</a> and the Gospel." But this is not common to all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>; because, as it is written (<a href="../bible/rom010.htm#verse16">Romans 10:16</a>), "all do not obey the gospel." Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not the same in all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, "Things which are according to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> are said to be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>," as stated in Ethic. v. But it is stated in the same book that nothing is so universally just as not to be subject to change in regard to some men. Therefore even the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not the same in all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, as stated above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>,<a href="#article3">Article 3</a>), to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> belongs everything to which a man is inclined according to his <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>. Now different men are <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> inclined to different things; some to the desire of pleasures, others to the desire of honors, and other men to other things. Therefore there is not one <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> for all.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 4): "The <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is common to all <a href="../cathen/06422a.htm">nations</a>."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>,<a href="#article3">Article 3</a>), to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> belongs those things to which a man is inclined <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a>: and among these it is proper to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> to be inclined to act according to <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>. Now the process of reason is from the common to the proper, as stated in Phys. i. The speculative reason, however, is differently situated in this matter, from the practical reason. For, since the speculative reason is busied chiefly with the <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> things, which cannot be otherwise than they are, its proper conclusions, like the universal principles, contain the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> without fail. The practical reason, on the other hand, is busied with contingent matters, about which <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions are concerned: and consequently, although there is <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> in the general principles, the more we descend to matters of detail, the more frequently we encounter defects. Accordingly then in speculative matters <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> is the same in all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, both as to principles and as to conclusions: although the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> is not <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all as regards the conclusions, but only as regards the principles which are called common notions. But in matters of action, <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> or practical rectitude is not the same for all, as to matters of detail, but only as to the general principles: and where there is the same rectitude in matters of detail, it is not equally <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all.</p>

<p>It is therefore evident that, as regards the general principles whether of speculative or of practical reason, <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> or rectitude is the same for all, and is equally <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> by all. As to the proper conclusions of the speculative reason, the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> is the same for all, but is not equally <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all: thus it is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> for all that the three angles of a triangle are together equal to two right angles, although it is not <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all. But as to the proper conclusions of the practical reason, neither is the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> or rectitude the same for all, nor, where it is the same, is it equally <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> by all. Thus it is right and <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> for all to act according to reason: and from this principle it follows as a proper conclusion, that goods entrusted to another should be restored to their owner. Now this is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> for the majority of cases: but it may happen in a particular case that it would be injurious, and therefore unreasonable, to restore goods held in trust; for instance, if they are claimed for the purpose of fighting against one's country. And this principle will be found to fail the more, according as we descend further into detail, e.g. if one were to say that goods held in trust should be restored with such and such a guarantee, or in such and such a way; because the greater the number of <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> added, the greater the number of ways in which the principle may fail, so that it be not right to restore or not to restore.</p>

<p>Consequently we must say that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as to general principles, is the same for all, both as to rectitude and as to <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knowledge</a>. But as to certain matters of detail, which are conclusions, as it were, of those general principles, it is the same for all in the majority of cases, both as to rectitude and as to <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knowledge</a>; and yet in some few cases it may fail, both as to rectitude, by reason of certain obstacles (just as natures subject to generation and corruption fail in some few cases on account of some obstacle), and as to <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knowledge</a>, since in some the reason is perverted by passion, or <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>, or an <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> disposition of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>; thus formerly, <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a>, although it is expressly contrary to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, was not considered wrong among the Germans, as Julius Caesar relates (De Bello Gall. vi).</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The meaning of the sentence quoted is not that whatever is contained in the <a href="../cathen/10582c.htm">Law</a> and the Gospel belongs to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, since they contain many things that are above <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>; but that whatever belongs to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is fully contained in them. Wherefore Gratian, after saying that "the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is what is contained in the <a href="../cathen/10582c.htm">Law</a> and the Gospel," adds at once, by way of example, "by which everyone is commanded to do to others as he would be done by."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> The saying of the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> is to be understood of things that are <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, not as general principles, but as conclusions drawn from them, having rectitude in the majority of cases, but failing in a few.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> As, in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, reason rules and commands the other powers, so all the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> inclinations belonging to the other powers must needs be directed according to <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>. Wherefore it is universally right for all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, that all their inclinations should be directed according to <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>.</p>

<h2 id="article5">Article 5. Whether the natural law can be changed?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> can be changed. Because on <a href="../bible/sir017.htm#verse9">Sirach 17:9</a>, "He gave them instructions, and the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of life," the <a href="../cathen/06586a.htm">gloss</a> says: "He wished the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of the letter to be written, in order to correct the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>." But that which is corrected is changed. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> can be changed.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the slaying of the innocent, <a href="../cathen/01163a.htm">adultery</a>, and <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a> are against the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. But we find these things changed by <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>: as when <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> commanded <a href="../cathen/01051a.htm">Abraham</a> to slay his innocent son (<a href="../bible/gen022.htm#verse2">Genesis 22:2</a>); and when he ordered the <a href="../cathen/08386a.htm">Jews</a> to borrow and purloin the vessels of the Egyptians (<a href="../bible/exo012.htm#verse35">Exodus 12:35</a>); and when He commanded Osee to take to himself "a wife of fornications" (<a href="../bible/hos001.htm#verse2">Hosea 1:2</a>). Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> can be changed.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. 5:4) that "the possession of all things in common, and universal freedom, are matters of <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>." But these things are seen to be changed by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws. Therefore it seems that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is subject to change.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> It is said in the Decretals (Dist. v): "The <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> dates from the creation of the rational creature. It does not vary according to time, but remains unchangeable."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> A change in the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> may be understood in two ways. First, by way of addition. In this sense nothing hinders the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> from being changed: since many things for the benefit of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> life have been added over and above the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, both by the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a> and by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws.</p>

<p>Secondly, a change in the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> may be understood by way of subtraction, so that what previously was according to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, ceases to be so. In this sense, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is altogether unchangeable in its first principles: but in its secondary principles, which, as we have said (<a href="#article4">Article 4</a>), are certain detailed proximate conclusions drawn from the first principles, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is not changed so that what it prescribes be not right in most cases. But it may be changed in some particular cases of rare occurrence, through some special <a href="../cathen/03459a.htm">causes</a> hindering the observance of such precepts, as stated above (<a href="#article4">Article 4</a>).</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The written <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is said to be given for the correction of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, either because it supplies what was wanting to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>; or because the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> was perverted in the hearts of some men, as to certain matters, so that they esteemed those things <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> which are <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">naturally</a> <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>; which perversion stood in need of correction.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> All men alike, both guilty and innocent, die the death of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>: which death of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> is inflicted by the power of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> on account of <a href="../cathen/11312a.htm">original sin</a>, according to <a href="../bible/1sa002.htm#verse6">1 Samuel 2:6</a>: "The Lord killeth and maketh alive." Consequently, by the command of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, death can be inflicted on any <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, guilty or innocent, without any <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">injustice</a> whatever. In like manner <a href="../cathen/01163a.htm">adultery</a> is intercourse with another's wife; who is allotted to him by the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> emanating from <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>. Consequently intercourse with any <a href="../cathen/15687b.htm">woman</a>, by the command of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, is neither <a href="../cathen/01163a.htm">adultery</a> nor fornication. The same applies to <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a>, which is the taking of another's property. For whatever is taken by the command of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, to Whom all things belong, is not taken against the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a> of its owner, whereas it is in this that <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a> consists. Nor is it only in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> things, that whatever is commanded by <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> is right; but also in <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> things, whatever is done by <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, is, in some way, <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a>, as stated in the <a href="../summa/1105.htm#article6">I:105:6 ad 1</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> A thing is said to belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> in two ways. First, because <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> inclines thereto: e.g. that one should not do harm to another. Secondly, because <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> did not bring in the contrary: thus we might say that for <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> to be naked is of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, because <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> did not give him clothes, but art invented them. In this sense, "the possession of all things in common and universal freedom" are said to be of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, because, to wit, the distinction of possessions and slavery were not brought in by <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, but devised by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a> for the benefit of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> life. Accordingly the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> was not changed in this respect, except by addition.</p>

<h2 id="article6">Article 6. Whether the law of nature can be abolished from the heart of man?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> can be abolished from the heart of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>. Because on <a href="../bible/rom002.htm#verse14">Romans 2:14</a>, "When the <a href="../cathen/06422a.htm">Gentiles</a> who have not the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>," etc. a <a href="../cathen/06586a.htm">gloss</a> says that "the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of righteousness, which <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sin</a> had blotted out, is graven on the heart of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> when he is restored by <a href="../cathen/06689a.htm">grace</a>." But the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of righteousness is the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> can be blotted out.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of <a href="../cathen/06689a.htm">grace</a> is more efficacious than the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>. But the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of <a href="../cathen/06689a.htm">grace</a> is blotted out by <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sin</a>. Much more therefore can the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> be blotted out.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, that which is established by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is made just. But many things are enacted by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, which are contrary to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> can be abolished from the heart of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (Confess. ii): "Thy <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is written in the hearts of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, which <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">iniquity</a> itself effaces not." But the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> which is written in men's hearts is the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> cannot be blotted out.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="#article4">Article 4</a>,<a href="#article5">Article 5</a>), there belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, first, certain most general precepts, that are <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> to all; and secondly, certain secondary and more detailed precepts, which are, as it were, conclusions following closely from first principles. As to those general principles, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, in the <a href="../cathen/01074a.htm">abstract</a>, can nowise be blotted out from men's hearts. But it is blotted out in the case of a particular action, in so far as reason is hindered from applying the general principle to a particular point of practice, on account of <a href="../cathen/04208a.htm">concupiscence</a> or some other passion, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2077.htm#article2">I-II:77:2</a>). But as to the other, i.e. the secondary precepts, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> can be blotted out from the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> heart, either by <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> persuasions, just as in speculative matters <a href="../cathen/05525a.htm">errors</a> occur in respect of <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> conclusions; or by <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vicious</a> customs and corrupt <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habits</a>, as among some men, <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a>, and even unnatural <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, as the <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> states (<a href="../bible/rom001.htm">Romans 1</a>), were not esteemed <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sinful</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Sin blots out the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> in particular cases, not universally, except perchance in regard to the secondary precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, in the way stated above.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> Although <a href="../cathen/06689a.htm">grace</a> is more efficacious than <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, yet <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> is more <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">essential</a> to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, and therefore more enduring.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> This argument is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> of the secondary precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, against which some legislators have framed certain enactments which are <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a>.</p>

<div class='catholicadnet-728x90' id='summa-728x90-top' style='display: flex; height: 100px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; '></div>

<h1>Question 95. Human law</h1>

<ol><li><a href="../summa/2095.htm#article1"> Its utility</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2095.htm#article2"> Its origin</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2095.htm#article3"> Its quality</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2095.htm#article4"> Its division</a> </li></ol>

<h2 id="article1">Article 1. Whether it was useful for laws to be framed by men?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that it was not useful for laws to be framed by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>. Because the purpose of every <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> be made <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> thereby, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2092.htm#article1">I-II:92:1</a>). But men are more to be induced to be <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> willingly by means of admonitions, than against their will, by means of laws. Therefore there was no need to frame laws.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 4), "men have recourse to a judge as to animate <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a>." But animate <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a> is better than inanimate <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a>, which contained in laws. Therefore it would have been better for the execution of <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a> to be entrusted to the decision of judges, than to frame laws in addition.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, every <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is framed for the direction of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions, as is evident from what has been stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>). But since <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions are about singulars, which are <a href="../cathen/08004a.htm">infinite</a> in number, <a href="../cathen/10053b.htm">matter</a> pertaining to the direction of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions cannot be taken into sufficient consideration except by a wise <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, who looks into each one of them. Therefore it would have been better for <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a> to be directed by the judgment of wise men, than by the framing of laws. Therefore there was no need of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 20): "Laws were made that in fear thereof <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> audacity might be held in check, that innocence might be safeguarded in the midst of <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wickedness</a>, and that the dread of punishment might prevent the <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a> from doing harm." But these things are most <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">mankind</a>. Therefore it was <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws should be made.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2063.htm#article1">I-II:63:1</a>; <a href="../summa/2094.htm#article3">I-II:94:3</a>), <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> has a <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> aptitude for <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>; but the perfection of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> must be acquired by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> by means of some kind of training. Thus we observe that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is helped by industry in his necessities, for instance, in food and clothing. Certain beginnings of these he has from <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, viz. his <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a> and his hands; but he has not the full complement, as other animals have, to whom <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> has given sufficiency of clothing and food. Now it is difficult to see how <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> could suffice for himself in the <a href="../cathen/10053b.htm">matter</a> of this training: since the perfection of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> consists chiefly in withdrawing <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> from undue pleasures, to which above all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is inclined, and especially the young, who are more capable of being trained. Consequently a man needs to receive this training from another, whereby to arrive at the perfection of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. And as to those young people who are inclined to acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, by their <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> disposition, or by custom, or rather by the <a href="../cathen/06553a.htm">gift</a> of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, paternal training suffices, which is by admonitions. But since some are found to be depraved, and prone to <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vice</a>, and not easily amenable to words, it was <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> for such to be restrained from <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> by force and fear, in order that, at least, they might desist from <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>-doing, and leave others in peace, and that they themselves, by being habituated in this way, might be brought to do willingly what hitherto they did from fear, and thus become <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>. Now this kind of training, which compels through fear of punishment, is the discipline of laws. Therefore in order that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> might have peace and <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, it was <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> for laws to be framed: for, as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Polit. i, 2), "as <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is the most noble of animals if he be perfect in <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, so is he the lowest of all, if he be severed from <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> and righteousness"; because <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> can use his <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a> to devise means of satisfying his lusts and <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> <a href="../cathen/11534a.htm">passions</a>, which other animals are unable to do.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Men who are well disposed are led willingly to <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> by being admonished better than by coercion: but men who are <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evilly</a> disposed are not led to <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> unless they are compelled.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> As the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Rhet. i, 1), "it is better that all things be regulated by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, than left to be decided by judges": and this for three reasons. First, because it is easier to find a few wise men competent to frame right laws, than to find the many who would be <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> to judge aright of each single case. Secondly, because those who make laws consider long beforehand what laws to make; whereas judgment on each single case has to be pronounced as soon as it arises: and it is easier for <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> to see what is right, by taking many instances into consideration, than by considering one solitary fact. Thirdly, because lawgivers judge in the abstract and of future events; whereas those who sit in judgment of things present, towards which they are affected by love, <a href="../cathen/07149b.htm">hatred</a>, or some kind of cupidity; wherefore their judgment is perverted.</p>

<p>Since then the animated <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a> of the judge is not found in every <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, and since it can be deflected, therefore it was <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a>, whenever possible, for the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to determine how to judge, and for very few matters to be left to the decision of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> Certain <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> facts which cannot be covered by the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> "have <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessarily</a> to be committed to judges," as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says in the same passage: for instance, "concerning something that has happened or not happened," and the like.</p>

<h2 id="article2">Article 2. Whether every human law is derived from the natural law?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that not every <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. For the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 7) that "the legal just is that which originally was a matter of indifference." But those things which arise from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> are not matters of indifference. Therefore the enactments of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws are not derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, positive <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is contrasted with <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as stated by <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> (Etym. v, 4) and the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> (Ethic. v, 7). But those things which flow as conclusions from the general principles of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2094.htm#article4">I-II:94:4</a>). Therefore that which is established by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not belong to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> is the same for all; since the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 7) that "the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> just is that which is equally valid everywhere." If therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws were derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, it would follow that they too are the same for all: which is clearly <a href="../cathen/05781a.htm">false</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 4.</strong> Further, it is possible to give a reason for things which are derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>. But "it is not possible to give the reason for all the legal enactments of the lawgivers," as the jurist says [Pandect. Justin. lib. i, ff, tit. iii, v; De Leg. et Senat.]. Therefore not all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws are derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> Tully says (Rhet. ii): "Things which emanated from <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> and were approved by custom, were sanctioned by fear and reverence for the laws."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Lib. Arb. i, 5) "that which is not just seems to be no <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> at all": wherefore the force of a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> depends on the extent of its <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a>. Now in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> affairs a thing is said to be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, from being right, according to the rule of reason. But the first rule of reason is the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, as is clear from what has been stated above (<a href="../summa/2091.htm#article2">I-II:91:2 ad 2</a>). Consequently every <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> has just so much of the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as it is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>. But if in any point it deflects from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, it is no longer a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> but a perversion of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p>But it must be noted that something may be derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> in two ways: first, as a conclusion from premises, secondly, by way of determination of certain generalities. The first way is like to that by which, in <a href="../cathen/13598b.htm">sciences</a>, demonstrated conclusions are drawn from the principles: while the second mode is likened to that whereby, in the arts, general forms are particularized as to details: thus the craftsman needs to determine the general form of a house to some particular shape. Some things are therefore derived from the general principles of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, by way of conclusions; e.g. that "one must not kill" may be derived as a conclusion from the principle that "one should do harm to no <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>": while some are derived therefrom by way of determination; e.g. the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> has it that the evil-doer should be punished; but that he be punished in this or that way, is a determination of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>.</p>

<p>Accordingly both modes of derivation are found in the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. But those things which are derived in the first way, are contained in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> not as emanating therefrom exclusively, but have some force from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> also. But those things which are derived in the second way, have no other force than that of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> is speaking of those enactments which are by way of determination or specification of the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> This argument avails for those things that are derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, by way of conclusions.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> The general principles of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> cannot be applied to all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> in the same way on account of the great variety of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> affairs: and hence arises the diversity of positive laws among various people.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 4.</strong> These words of the Jurist are to be understood as referring to decisions of rulers in determining particular points of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>: on which determinations the judgment of expert and <a href="../cathen/12517b.htm">prudent</a> men is based as on its principles; in so far, to wit, as they see at once what is the best thing to decide.</p>

<p>Hence the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. vi, 11) that in such matters, "we ought to pay as much attention to the undemonstrated sayings and opinions of <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a> who surpass us in experience, age and <a href="../cathen/12517b.htm">prudence</a>, as to their demonstrations."</p>

<h2 id="article3">Article 3. Whether Isidore's description of the quality of positive law is appropriate?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore's</a> description of the <a href="../cathen/12589c.htm">quality</a> of positive <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not appropriate, when he says (Etym. v, 21): "Law shall be <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>, <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, possible to <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, according to the custom of the country, suitable to place and time, <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a>, useful; clearly expressed, lest by its obscurity it lead to misunderstanding; framed for no private benefit, but for the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>." Because he had previously expressed the <a href="../cathen/12589c.htm">quality</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> in three <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a>, saying that "<a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is anything founded on reason, provided that it foster religion, be helpful to discipline, and further the common weal." Therefore it was needless to add any further <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> to these.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, Justice is included in honesty, as Tully says (De Offic. vii). Therefore after saying "honest" it was superfluous to add "just."</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, written <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is condivided with custom, according to <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> (Etym. ii, 10). Therefore it should not be stated in the definition of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that it is "according to the custom of the country."</p>

<p><strong>Objection 4.</strong> Further, a thing may be <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> in two ways. It may be <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> simply, because it cannot be otherwise: and that which is <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> in this way, is not subject to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> judgment, wherefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not concerned with <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> of this kind. Again a thing may be <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a> for an end: and this <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> is the same as usefulness. Therefore it is superfluous to say both "<a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a>" and "useful."</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> stands the authority of <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a>.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> Whenever a thing is for an end, its <a href="../cathen/06137b.htm">form</a> must be determined proportionately to that end; as the form of a saw is such as to be suitable for cutting (Phys. ii, text. 88). Again, everything that is ruled and measured must have a form proportionate to its rule and measure. Now both these <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> are verified of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>: since it is both something ordained to an end; and is a rule or measure ruled or measured by a higher measure. And this higher measure is twofold, viz. the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a> and the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as explained above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>; <a href="../summa/2093.htm#article3">I-II:93:3</a>). Now the end of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is to be useful to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, as the jurist states [Pandect. Justin. lib. xxv, ff., tit. iii; De Leg. et Senat.]. Wherefore <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> in determining the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, lays down, at first, three <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a>; viz. that it "foster religion," inasmuch as it is proportionate to the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>; that it be "helpful to discipline," inasmuch as it is proportionate to the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; and that it "further the common weal," inasmuch as it is proportionate to the utility of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">mankind</a>.</p>

<p>All the other <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> mentioned by him are reduced to these three. For it is called <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> because it fosters religion. And when he goes on to say that it should be "<a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, possible to <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, according to the customs of the country, adapted to place and time," he implies that it should be helpful to discipline. For <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> discipline depends on first on the order of <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>, to which he refers by saying "just": secondly, it depends on the ability of the agent; because discipline should be adapted to each one according to his ability, taking also into account the ability of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> (for the same burdens should be not laid on children as adults); and should be according to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> customs; since <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> cannot live alone in society, paying no heed to others: thirdly, it depends on certain circumstances, in respect of which he says, "adapted to place and time." The remaining words, "<a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessary</a>, useful," etc. mean that <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should further the common weal: so that "<a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a>" refers to the removal of <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a>; "usefulness" to the attainment of <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>; "clearness of expression," to the need of preventing any harm ensuing from the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> itself. And since, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article2">I-II:90:2</a>), <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, this is expressed in the last part of the description.</p>

<p>This suffices for the Replies to the Objections.</p>

<h2 id="article4">Article 4. Whether Isidore's division of human laws is appropriate?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> wrongly divided <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> statutes or <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> (Etym. v, 4, seqq.). For under this <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> he includes the "<a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of <a href="../cathen/06422a.htm">nations</a>," so called, because, as he says, "nearly all nations use it." But as he says, "<a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is that which is common to all <a href="../cathen/06422a.htm">nations</a>." Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of nations is not contained under positive <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, but rather under <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, those laws which have the same force, seem to differ not formally but only materially. But "statutes, decrees of the commonalty, senatorial decrees," and the like which he mentions (Etym. v, 9), all have the same force. Therefore they do not differ, except materially. But art takes no notice of such a distinction: since it may go on to <a href="../cathen/08004a.htm">infinity</a>. Therefore this division of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws is not appropriate.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, just as, in the state, there are princes, <a href="../cathen/12406a.htm">priests</a> and soldiers, so are there other <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> offices. Therefore it seems that, as this division includes "military <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>," and "public <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>," referring to <a href="../cathen/12406a.htm">priests</a> and magistrates; so also it should include other laws pertaining to other offices of the state.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 4.</strong> Further, those things that are <a href="../cathen/01096c.htm">accidental</a> should be passed over. But it is <a href="../cathen/01096c.htm">accidental</a> to <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that it be framed by this or that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>. Therefore it is unreasonable to divide laws according to the names of lawgivers, so that one be called the "Cornelian" <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, another the "Falcidian" <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, etc.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The authority of <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> (Objection 1) suffices.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> A thing can of itself be divided in respect of something contained in the notion of that thing. Thus a <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a> either rational or irrational is contained in the notion of animal: and therefore animal is divided properly and of itself in respect of its being rational or irrational; but not in the point of its being white or black, which are entirely beside the notion of animal. Now, in the notion of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, many things are contained, in respect of any of which <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> can be divided properly and of itself. For in the first place it belongs to the notion of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, to be derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, as explained above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>). In this respect positive <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is divided into the "<a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of <a href="../cathen/06422a.htm">nations</a>" and <a href="../cathen/09066a.htm">"civil law"</a>, according to the two ways in which something may be derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, as stated above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>). Because, to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of nations belong those things which are derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, as conclusions from premises, e.g. just buyings and sellings, and the like, without which men cannot live together, which is a point of the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>, since <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is by <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> a social animal, as is <a href="../cathen/12454c.htm">proved</a> in Polit. i, 2. But those things which are derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> by way of particular determination, belong to the <a href="../cathen/09066a.htm">civil law</a>, according as each state decides on what is best for itself.</p>

<p>Secondly, it belongs to the notion of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, to be ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of the state. In this respect <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> may be divided according to the different kinds of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> who work in a special way for the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>: e.g. <a href="../cathen/12406a.htm">priests</a>, by <a href="../cathen/12345b.htm">praying</a> to <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> for the people; princes, by governing the people; soldiers, by fighting for the safety of the people. Wherefore certain special kinds of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> are adapted to these men.</p>

<p>Thirdly, it belongs to the notion of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, to be framed by that one who governs the community of the state, as shown above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article3">I-II:90:3</a>). In this respect, there are various <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws according to the various forms of government. Of these, according to the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> (Polit. iii, 10) one is "monarchy," i.e. when the state is governed by one; and then we have "Royal Ordinances." Another form is "aristocracy," i.e. government by the best men or men of highest rank; and then we have the "Authoritative legal opinions" [Responsa Prudentum] and "Decrees of the Senate" [Senatus consulta]. Another form is "oligarchy," i.e. government by a few rich and powerful men; and then we have "Praetorian," also called "Honorary," <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Another form of government is that of the people, which is called "democracy," and there we have "Decrees of the commonalty" [Plebiscita]. There is also tyrannical government, which is altogether corrupt, which, therefore, has no corresponding <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Finally, there is a form of government made up of all these, and which is the best: and in this respect we have <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> sanctioned by the "Lords and Commons," as stated by <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> (Etym. v, 4, seqq.).</p>

<p>Fourthly, it belongs to the notion of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to direct <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> actions. In this respect, according to the various matters of which the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> treats, there are various kinds of laws, which are sometimes named after their authors: thus we have the "Lex Julia" about <a href="../cathen/01163a.htm">adultery</a>, the "Lex Cornelia" concerning assassins, and so on, differentiated in this way, not on account of the authors, but on account of the matters to which they refer.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of nations is indeed, in some way, <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, in so far as he is a reasonable being, because it is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> by way of a conclusion that is not very remote from its premises. Wherefore men easily agreed thereto. Nevertheless it is distinct from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, especially it is distinct from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> which is common to all animals.</p>

<p>The Replies to the other Objections are evident from what has been said.</p>
