<div class='catholicadnet-728x90' id='summa-728x90-top' style='display: flex; height: 100px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; '></div>

<h1>Question 96. The power of human law</h1>

<ol><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article1"> Should human law be framed for the community?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article2"> Should human law repress all vices?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article3"> Is human law competent to direct all acts of virtue?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article4"> Does it bind man in conscience?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article5"> Are all men subject to human law?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2096.htm#article6"> May those who are under the law act beside the letter of the law?</a> </li></ol>

<h2 id="article1">Article 1. Whether human law should be framed for the community rather than for the individual?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should be framed not for the community, but rather for the <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>. For the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 7) that "the legal just .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. includes all particular acts of legislation .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. and all those matters which are the subject of decrees," which are also <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> matters, since decrees are framed about <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> actions. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is framed not only for the community, but also for the <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is the director of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>). But <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a> are about <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> matters. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws should be framed, not for the community, but rather for the <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is a rule and measure of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>). But a measure should be most certain, as stated in Metaph. x. Since therefore in <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a> no general proposition can be so certain as not to fail in some <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> cases, it seems that laws should be framed not in general but for <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> cases.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The jurist says (Pandect. Justin. lib. i, tit. iii, art. ii; De legibus, etc.) that "laws should be made to suit the majority of instances; and they are not framed according to what may possibly happen in an <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> case."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> Whatever is for an end should be proportionate to that end. Now the end of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>; because, as <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 21) that "<a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should be framed, not for any private benefit, but for the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of all the citizens." Hence <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws should be proportionate to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. Now the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> comprises many things. Wherefore <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should take account of many things, as to <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a>, as to matters, and as to times. Because the community of the state is composed of many <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a>; and its <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> is procured by many actions; nor is it established to endure for only a short time, but to last for all time by the citizens succeeding one another, as <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Civ. Dei ii, 21; xxii, 6).</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> (Ethic. v, 7) divides the legal <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, i.e. positive <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, into three parts. For some things are laid down simply in a general way: and these are the general laws. Of these he says that "the legal is that which originally was a matter of indifference, but which, when enacted, is so no longer": as the fixing of the ransom of a captive. Some things affect the community in one respect, and <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individuals</a> in another. These are called "privileges," i.e. "private laws," as it were, because they regard private <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a>, although their power extends to many matters; and in regard to these, he adds, "and further, all particular acts of legislation." Other matters are legal, not through being laws, but through being applications of general laws to particular cases: such are decrees which have the force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; and in regard to these, he adds "all matters subject to decrees."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> A principle of direction should be applicable to many; wherefore (Metaph. x, text. 4) the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says that all things belonging to one genus, are measured by one, which is the principle in that genus. For if there were as many rules or measures as there are things measured or ruled, they would cease to be of use, since their use consists in being applicable to many things. Hence <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> would be of no use, if it did not extend further than to one single act. Because the decrees than to one single act. Because the decrees of <a href="../cathen/12517b.htm">prudent</a> men are made for the purpose of directing <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> actions; whereas <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is a general precept, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2092.htm#article2">I-II:92:2 Objection 2</a>).</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> "We must not seek the same degree of <a href="../cathen/03539b.htm">certainty</a> in all things" (Ethic. i, 3). Consequently in contingent matters, such as <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> and <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> things, it is enough for a thing to be certain, as being <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> in the greater number of instances, though at times and less frequently it fail.</p>

<h2 id="article2">Article 2. Whether it belongs to the human law to repress all vices?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that it belongs to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to repress all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>. For <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 20) that "laws were made in order that, in fear thereof, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man's</a> audacity might be held in check." But it would not be held in check sufficiently, unless all <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a> were repressed by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws should repress all <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver is to make the citizens <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>. But a man cannot be <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> unless he forbear from all kinds of <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vice</a>. Therefore it belongs to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to repress all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2095.htm#article2">I-II:95:2</a>). But all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a> are contrary to the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should repress all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> We read in De Lib. Arb. i, 5: "It seems to me that the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> which is written for the governing of the people rightly permits these things, and that <a href="../cathen/12510a.htm">Divine providence</a> punishes them." But <a href="../cathen/12510a.htm">Divine providence</a> punishes nothing but <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> rightly allows some <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, by not repressing them.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>), <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is framed as a rule or measure of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>. Now a measure should be homogeneous with that which it measures, as stated in Metaph. x, text. 3,4, since different things are measured by different measures. Wherefore laws imposed on men should also be in keeping with their <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">condition</a>, for, as <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 21), <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should be "possible both according to <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, and according to the customs of the country." Now possibility or faculty of action is due to an interior <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> or disposition: since the same thing is not possible to one who has not a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a>, as is possible to one who has. Thus the same is not possible to a child as to a full-grown <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>: for which reason the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> for children is not the same as for adults, since many things are permitted to children, which in an adult are punished by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> or at any rate are open to blame. In like manner many things are permissible to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> not perfect in <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, which would be intolerable in a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>.</p>

<p>Now <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is framed for a number of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> beings, the majority of whom are not perfect in <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. Wherefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws do not forbid all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, from which the <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> abstain, but only the more grievous <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, from which it is possible for the majority to abstain; and chiefly those that are to the hurt of others, without the prohibition of which <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> society could not be maintained: thus <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> prohibits <a href="../cathen/07441a.htm">murder</a>, <a href="../cathen/14564b.htm">theft</a> and such like.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Audacity seems to refer to the assailing of others. Consequently it belongs to those <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a> chiefly whereby one's neighbor is injured: and these <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sins</a> are forbidden by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as stated.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> The purpose of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is to lead men to <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, not suddenly, but gradually. Wherefore it does not lay upon the multitude of imperfect men the burdens of those who are already <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>, viz. that they should abstain from all <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>. Otherwise these imperfect ones, being unable to bear such precepts, would break out into yet greater <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a>: thus it is written (<a href="../bible/pro030.htm#verse33">Proverbs 30:33</a>): "He that violently bloweth his nose, bringeth out blood"; and (<a href="../bible/mat009.htm#verse17">Matthew 9:17</a>) that if "new wine," i.e. precepts of a perfect life, "is put into old bottles," i.e. into imperfect men, "the bottles break, and the wine runneth out," i.e. the precepts are despised, and those men, from contempt, break into <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a> worse still.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is a participation in us of the <a href="../cathen/05551b.htm">eternal</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>: while <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> falls short of the <a href="../cathen/05551b.htm">eternal</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Now <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Lib. Arb. i, 5): "The <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> which is framed for the government of states, allows and leaves unpunished many things that are punished by <a href="../cathen/12510a.htm">Divine providence</a>. Nor, if this <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not attempt to do everything, is this a reason why it should be blamed for what it does." Wherefore, too, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prohibit everything that is forbidden by the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>.</p>

<h2 id="article3">Article 3. Whether human law prescribes acts of all the virtues?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prescribe acts of all the <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a>. For <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vicious</a> acts are contrary to acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. But <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prohibit all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, as stated above (<a href="#article2">Article 2</a>). Therefore neither does it prescribe all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> act proceeds from a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. But <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> is the end of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; so that whatever is from a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>, cannot come under a precept of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prescribe all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article2">I-II:90:2</a>). But some acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> are ordained, not to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, but to private <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prescribe all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 1) that the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> "prescribes the performance of the acts of a brave <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. and the acts of the temperate <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. and the acts of the meek <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>: and in like manner as regards the other <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a> and <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vices</a>, prescribing the former, forbidding the latter."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> The <a href="../cathen/14210a.htm">species</a> of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a> are distinguished by their objects, as explained above (<a href="../summa/2054.htm#article2">I-II:54:2</a>; <a href="../summa/2060.htm#article1">I-II:60:1</a>; <a href="../summa/2062.htm#article2">I-II:62:2</a>). Now all the objects of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a> can be referred either to the private <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of an <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>, or to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of the multitude: thus matters of <a href="../cathen/06147a.htm">fortitude</a> may be achieved either for the safety of the state, or for upholding the rights of a friend, and in like manner with the other <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtues</a>. But <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article2">I-II:90:2</a>) is ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. Wherefore there is no <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> whose acts cannot be prescribed by the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Nevertheless <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not prescribe concerning all the acts of every <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>: but only in regard to those that are ordainable to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>&#8212;either immediately, as when certain things are done directly for the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>&#8212;or mediately, as when a lawgiver prescribes certain things pertaining to <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> order, whereby the citizens are directed in the upholding of the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a> and peace.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">Human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not forbid all <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vicious</a> acts, by the <a href="../cathen/11189a.htm">obligation</a> of a precept, as neither does it prescribe all acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. But it forbids certain acts of each <a href="../cathen/15403c.htm">vice</a>, just as it prescribes some acts of each <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> An act is said to be an act of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> in two ways. First, from the fact that a man does something <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a>; thus the act of <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justice</a> is to do what is right, and an act of <a href="../cathen/06147a.htm">fortitude</a> is to do brave things: and in this way <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> prescribes certain acts of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>. Secondly an act of <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> is when a man does a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> thing in a way in which a <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> does it. Such an act always proceeds from <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a>: and it does not come under a precept of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, but is the end at which every lawgiver aims.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> There is no <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtue</a> whose act is not ordainable to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, as stated above, either mediately or immediately.</p>

<h2 id="article4">Article 4. Whether human law binds a man in conscience?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not bind <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>. For an inferior power has no <a href="../cathen/08567a.htm">jurisdiction</a> in a court of higher power. But the power of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, which frames <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, is beneath the Divine power. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> cannot impose its precept in a Divine court, such as is the court of <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the judgment of <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a> depends chiefly on the commandments of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>. But sometimes <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God's</a> commandments are made void by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws, according to <a href="../bible/mat015.htm#verse6">Matthew 15:6</a>: "You have made void the commandment of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> for your tradition." Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not bind a man in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws often bring loss of character and injury on <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, according to <a href="../bible/isa010.htm#verse1">Isaiah 10:1 et seqq.</a>: "Woe to them that make <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a> laws, and when they write, write <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">injustice</a>; to oppress the poor in judgment, and do <a href="../cathen/15446a.htm">violence</a> to the <a href="../cathen/03459a.htm">cause</a> of the <a href="../cathen/07543b.htm">humble</a> of My people." But it is lawful for anyone to avoid oppression and <a href="../cathen/15446a.htm">violence</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws do not bind <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> It is written (<a href="../bible/1pe002.htm#verse19">1 Peter 2:19</a>): "This is thankworthy, if for <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a> .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. a man endure sorrows, suffering wrongfully."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> Laws framed by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> are either just or <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a>. If they be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, they have the power of binding in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>, from the <a href="../cathen/05551b.htm">eternal</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> whence they are derived, according to <a href="../bible/pro008.htm#verse15">Proverbs 8:15</a>: "By Me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." Now laws are said to be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, both from the end, when, to wit, they are ordained to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>&#8212;and from their author, that is to say, when the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that is made does not exceed the power of the lawgiver&#8212;and from their form, when, to wit, burdens are laid on the subjects, according to an equality of proportion and with a view to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. For, since one <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is a part of the community, each <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> in all that he is and has, belongs to the community; just as a part, in all that it is, belongs to the whole; wherefore <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> inflicts a loss on the part, in order to save the whole: so that on this account, such laws as these, which impose proportionate burdens, are just and binding in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>, and are legal laws.</p>

<p>On the other hand laws may be <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a> in two ways: first, by being contrary to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, through being opposed to the things mentioned above&#8212;either in respect of the end, as when an authority imposes on his subjects burdensome laws, conducive, not to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, but rather to his own cupidity or vainglory&#8212;or in respect of the author, as when a man makes a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that goes beyond the power committed to him&#8212;or in respect of the form, as when burdens are imposed unequally on the community, although with a view to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. The like are acts of <a href="../cathen/15446a.htm">violence</a> rather than laws; because, as <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Lib. Arb. i, 5), "a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that is not <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, seems to be no <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> at all." Wherefore such laws do not bind in <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>, except perhaps in order to avoid <a href="../cathen/13506d.htm">scandal</a> or disturbance, for which <a href="../cathen/03459a.htm">cause</a> a man should even yield his right, according to <a href="../bible/mat005.htm#verse40">Matthew 5:40-41</a>: "If a man .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. take away thy coat, let go thy cloak also unto him; and whosoever will force thee one mile, go with him other two."</p>

<p>Secondly, laws may be <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a> through being opposed to the Divine <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>: such are the laws of tyrants inducing to <a href="../cathen/07636a.htm">idolatry</a>, or to anything else contrary to the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>: and laws of this kind must nowise be observed, because, as stated in <a href="../bible/act005.htm#verse29">Acts 5:29</a>, "we ought to obey <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> rather than <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> As the <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> says (<a href="../bible/rom013.htm#verse1">Romans 13:1-2</a>), all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> power is from <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. "therefore he that resisteth the power," in matters that are within its scope, "resisteth the ordinance of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>"; so that he becomes guilty according to his <a href="../cathen/04268a.htm">conscience</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> This argument is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> of laws that are contrary to the commandments of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, which is beyond the scope of (<a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a>) power. Wherefore in such matters <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should not be obeyed.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> This argument is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> of a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that inflicts <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a> hurt on its subjects. The power that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> holds from <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> does not extend to this: wherefore neither in such matters is <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> bound to obey the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, provided he avoid giving <a href="../cathen/13506d.htm">scandal</a> or inflicting a more grievous hurt.</p>

<h2 id="article5">Article 5. Whether all are subject to the law?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that not all are subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. For those alone are subject to a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> for whom a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is made. But the <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> says (<a href="../bible/1ti001.htm#verse9">1 Timothy 1:9</a>): "The <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not made for the just <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>." Therefore the just are not subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, Pope Urban says [Decretals. caus. xix, qu. 2]: "He that is guided by a private <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> need not for any reason be bound by the public <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>." Now all <a href="../cathen/14220b.htm">spiritual</a> men are led by the private <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Holy Ghost</a>, for they are the sons of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, of whom it is said (<a href="../bible/rom008.htm#verse14">Romans 8:14</a>): "Whosoever are led by the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Spirit of God</a>, they are the sons of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>." Therefore not all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> are subject to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, the jurist says [Pandect. Justin. i, ff., tit. 3, De Leg. et Senat.] that "the sovereign is exempt from the laws." But he that is exempt from the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not bound thereby. Therefore not all are subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> says (<a href="../bible/rom013.htm#verse1">Romans 13:1</a>): "Let every <a href="../cathen/14153a.htm">soul</a> be subject to the higher powers." But subjection to a power seems to imply subjection to the laws framed by that power. Therefore all <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a> should be subject to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>; <a href="#article3">Article 3, Reply to Objection 2</a>), the notion of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> contains two things: first, that it is a rule of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>; secondly, that it has coercive power. Wherefore a man may be subject to <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> in two ways. First, as the regulated is subject to the regulator: and, in this way, whoever is subject to a power, is subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> framed by that power. But it may happen in two ways that one is not subject to a power. In one way, by being altogether free from its authority: hence the subjects of one city or kingdom are not bound by the laws of the sovereign of another city or kingdom, since they are not subject to his authority. In another way, by being under a yet higher <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; thus the subject of a proconsul should be ruled by his command, but not in those matters in which the subject receives his orders from the emperor: for in these matters, he is not bound by the mandate of the lower authority, since he is directed by that of a higher. In this way, one who is simply subject to a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, may not be a subject thereto in certain matters, in respect of which he is ruled by a higher <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p>Secondly, a man is said to be subject to a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> as the coerced is subject to the coercer. In this way the <a href="../cathen/15472a.htm">virtuous</a> and righteous are not subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, but only the <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a>. Because coercion and <a href="../cathen/15446a.htm">violence</a> are contrary to the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a>: but the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a> of the <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> is in harmony with the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, whereas the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a> of the <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a> is discordant from it. Wherefore in this sense the <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> are not subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, but only the <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> This argument is <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">true</a> of subjection by way of coercion: for, in this way, "the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not made for the just men": because "they are a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to themselves," since they "show the work of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> written in their hearts," as the <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> says (<a href="../bible/rom002.htm#verse14">Romans 2:14-15</a>). Consequently the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> does not enforce itself upon them as it does on the <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">wicked</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Holy Ghost</a> is above all <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> framed by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>: and therefore <a href="../cathen/14220b.htm">spiritual</a> men, in so far as they are led by the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Holy Ghost</a>, are not subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> in those matters that are inconsistent with the guidance of the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Holy Ghost</a>. Nevertheless the very fact that <a href="../cathen/14220b.htm">spiritual</a> men are subject to <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, is due to the leading of the <a href="../cathen/07409a.htm">Holy Ghost</a>, according to <a href="../bible/1pe002.htm#verse13">1 Peter 2:13</a>: "Be ye subject .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. to every <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> creature for <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God's</a> sake."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> The sovereign is said to be "exempt from the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>," as to its coercive power; since, properly speaking, no <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is coerced by himself, and <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> has no coercive power save from the authority of the sovereign. Thus then is the sovereign said to be exempt from the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, because none is competent to pass sentence on him, if he acts against the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Wherefore on <a href="../bible/psa050.htm#verse6">Psalm 50:6</a>: "To Thee only have I <a href="../cathen/14004b.htm">sinned</a>," a <a href="../cathen/06586a.htm">gloss</a> says that "there is no <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> who can judge the <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">deeds</a> of a king." But as to the directive force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, the sovereign is subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> by his own will, according to the statement (Extra, De Constit. cap. Cum omnes) that "whatever <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> a man makes for another, he should keep himself. And a wise authority [Dionysius Cato, Dist. de Moribus] says: 'Obey the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that thou makest thyself.'" Moreover the Lord reproaches those who "say and do not"; and who "bind heavy burdens and lay them on men's shoulders, but with a finger of their own they will not move them" (<a href="../bible/mat023.htm#verse3">Matthew 23:3-4</a>). Hence, in the judgment of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, the sovereign is not exempt from the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as to its directive force; but he should fulfil it to his own <a href="../cathen/06259a.htm">free-will</a> and not of constraint. Again the sovereign is above the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in so far as, when it is expedient, he can change the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, and dispense in it according to time and place.</p>

<h2 id="article6">Article 6. Whether he who is under a law may act beside the letter of the law?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It seems that he who is subject to a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> may not act beside the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. For <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Vera Relig. 31): "Although men judge about temporal laws when they make them, yet when once they are made they must pass judgment not on them, but according to them." But if anyone disregard the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, saying that he observes the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver, he seems to pass judgment on the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Therefore it is not right for one who is under the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to disregard the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in order to observe the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, he alone is competent to interpret the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> who can make the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. But those who are subject to the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> cannot make the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Therefore they have no right to interpret the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver, but should always act according to the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, every wise <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knows</a> how to explain his <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> by words. But those who framed the laws should be reckoned wise: for Wisdom says (<a href="../bible/pro008.htm#verse15">Proverbs 8:15</a>): "By Me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." Therefore we should not judge of the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver otherwise than by the words of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/07349b.htm">Hilary</a> says (De Trin. iv): "The meaning of what is said is according to the motive for saying it: because things are not subject to speech, but speech to things." Therefore we should take account of the motive of the lawgiver, rather than of his very words.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="#article4">Article 4</a>), every <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is directed to the common weal of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">men</a>, and derives the force and <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> accordingly. Hence the jurist says [Pandect. Justin. lib. i, ff., tit. 3, De Leg. et Senat.]: "By no reason of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, or favor of equity, is it allowable for us to interpret harshly, and render burdensome, those useful measures which have been enacted for the welfare of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>." Now it happens often that the observance of some point of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> conduces to the common weal in the majority of instances, and yet, in some cases, is very hurtful. Since then the lawgiver cannot have in view every single case, he shapes the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> according to what happens most frequently, by directing his attention to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. Wherefore if a case arise wherein the observance of that <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> would be hurtful to the general welfare, it should not be observed. For instance, suppose that in a besieged city it be an established <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that the gates of the city are to be kept closed, this is <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> for public welfare as a general rule: but, it were to happen that the enemy are in pursuit of certain citizens, who are defenders of the city, it would be a great loss to the city, if the gates were not opened to them: and so in that case the gates ought to be opened, contrary to the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in order to maintain the common weal, which the lawgiver had in view.</p>

<p>Nevertheless it must be noted, that if the observance of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> according to the letter does not involve any sudden risk needing instant remedy, it is not competent for everyone to expound what is useful and what is not useful to the state: those alone can do this who are in authority, and who, on account of such like cases, have the power to dispense from the laws. If, however, the peril be so sudden as not to allow of the delay involved by referring the <a href="../cathen/10053b.htm">matter</a> to authority, the mere <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> brings with it a <a href="../cathen/05041a.htm">dispensation</a>, since <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knows</a> no <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> He who in a case of <a href="../cathen/10733a.htm">necessity</a> acts beside the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, does not judge the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; but of a particular case in which he sees that the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not to be observed.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> He who follows the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of the lawgiver, does not interpret the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> simply; but in a case in which it is evident, by reason of the manifest harm, that the lawgiver intended otherwise. For if it be a matter of <a href="../cathen/05141a.htm">doubt</a>, he must either act according to the letter of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, or consult those in power.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> No <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is so wise as to be able to take account of every single case; wherefore he is not able sufficiently to express in words all those things that are suitable for the end he has in view. And even if a lawgiver were able to take all the cases into consideration, he ought not to mention them all, in order to avoid confusion: but should frame the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> according to that which is of most common occurrence.</p>

<div class='catholicadnet-728x90' id='summa-728x90-top' style='display: flex; height: 100px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; '></div>

<h1>Question 97. Change in laws</h1>

<ol><li><a href="../summa/2097.htm#article1"> Is human law changeable?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2097.htm#article2"> Should it be always changed, whenever anything better occurs?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2097.htm#article3"> Is it abolished by custom, and does custom obtain the force of law?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/2097.htm#article4"> Should the application of human law be changed by dispensation of those in authority?</a> </li></ol>

<h2 id="article1">Article 1. Whether human law should be changed in any way?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should not be changed in any way at all. Because <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2095.htm#article2">I-II:95:2</a>). But the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> endures unchangeably. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should also remain without any change.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. v, 5), a measure should be absolutely stable. But <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is the measure of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2090.htm#article1">Question 90, Articles 1 and 2</a>). Therefore it should remain without change.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, it is of the <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">essence</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to be just and right, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2095.htm#article2">I-II:95:2</a>). But that which is right once is right always. Therefore that which is <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> once, should be always <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (De Lib. Arb. i, 6): "A temporal <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, however <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, may be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">justly</a> changed in course of <a href="../cathen/14726a.htm">time</a>."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2091.htm#article3">I-II:91:3</a>), <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is a dictate of <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>, whereby <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a> are directed. Thus there may be two <a href="../cathen/03459a.htm">causes</a> for the just change of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>: one on the part of reason; the other on the part of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> whose acts are regulated by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. The <a href="../cathen/03459a.htm">cause</a> on the part of reason is that it seems <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a> to advance gradually from the imperfect to the perfect. Hence, in speculative <a href="../cathen/13598b.htm">sciences</a>, we see that the teaching of the early <a href="../cathen/12025c.htm">philosophers</a> was imperfect, and that it was afterwards perfected by those who succeeded them. So also in practical matters: for those who first endeavored to discover something useful for the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> community, not being able by themselves to take everything into consideration, set up certain institutions which were deficient in many ways; and these were changed by subsequent lawgivers who made institutions that might <a href="../cathen/12454c.htm">prove</a> less frequently deficient in respect of the common weal.</p>

<p>On the part of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, whose acts are regulated by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> can be rightly changed on account of the changed <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">condition</a> of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, to whom different things are expedient according to the difference of his condition. An example is proposed by <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> (De Lib. Arb. i, 6): "If the people have a sense of moderation and responsibility, and are most careful guardians of the common weal, it is right to enact a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> allowing such a people to choose their own magistrates for the government of the commonwealth. But if, as time goes on, the same people become so corrupt as to sell their votes, and entrust the government to scoundrels and criminals; then the right of appointing their public officials is rightly forfeit to such a people, and the choice devolves to a few <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> men."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> is a participation of the <a href="../cathen/05551b.htm">eternal</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2091.htm#article2">I-II:91:2</a>), and therefore endures without change, owing to the unchangeableness and perfection of the Divine <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">Reason</a>, the Author of <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>. But the reason of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is changeable and imperfect: wherefore his <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is subject to change. Moreover the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> contains certain universal precepts, which are everlasting: whereas <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> contains certain particular precepts, according to various emergencies.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> A measure should be as enduring as possible. But nothing can be absolutely unchangeable in things that are subject to change. And therefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> cannot be altogether unchangeable.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> In corporal things, right is predicated absolutely: and therefore, as far as itself is concerned, always remains right. But right is predicated of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> with reference to the common weal, to which one and the same thing is not always adapted, as stated above: wherefore rectitude of this kind is subject to change.</p>

<h2 id="article2">Article 2. Whether human law should always be changed, whenever something better occurs?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should be changed, whenever something better occurs. Because <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws are devised by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>, like other arts. But in the other arts, the tenets of former times give place to others, if something better occurs. Therefore the same should apply to <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, by taking note of the past we can provide for the future. Now unless <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws had been changed when it was found possible to improve them, considerable inconvenience would have ensued; because the laws of old were crude in many points. Therefore it seems that laws should be changed, whenever anything better occurs to be enacted.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws are enacted about single acts of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>. But we cannot acquire perfect <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knowledge</a> in singular matters, except by experience, which "requires time," as stated in Ethic. ii. Therefore it seems that as time goes on it is possible for something better to occur for legislation.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> It is stated in the Decretals (Dist. xii, 5): "It is absurd, and a detestable shame, that we should suffer those traditions to be changed which we have received from the fathers of old."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> As stated above (<a href="#article1">Article 1</a>), <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is rightly changed, in so far as such change is conducive to the common weal. But, to a certain extent, the mere change of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is of itself prejudicial to the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>: because custom avails much for the observance of laws, seeing that what is done contrary to general custom, even in slight matters, is looked upon as grave. Consequently, when a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is changed, the binding power of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is diminished, in so far as custom is abolished. Wherefore <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> should never be changed, unless, in some way or other, the common weal be compensated according to the extent of the harm done in this respect. Such compensation may arise either from some very great and every evident benefit conferred by the new enactment; or from the extreme urgency of the case, due to the fact that either the <a href="../cathen/05543b.htm">existing</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is clearly <a href="../cathen/08010c.htm">unjust</a>, or its observance extremely harmful. Wherefore the jurist says [Pandect. Justin. lib. i, ff., tit. 4, De Constit. Princip.] that "in establishing new laws, there should be evidence of the benefit to be derived, before departing from a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> which has long been considered just."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Rules of art derive their force from reason alone: and therefore whenever something better occurs, the rule followed hitherto should be changed. But "laws derive very great force from custom," as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> states (Polit. ii, 5): consequently they should not be quickly changed.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> This argument proves that laws ought to be changed: not in view of any improvement, but for the sake of a great benefit or in a case of great urgency, as stated above. This answer applies also to the Third Objection.</p>

<h2 id="article3">Article 3. Whether custom can obtain force of law?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that custom cannot obtain force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, nor abolish a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. Because <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is derived from the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">natural law</a> and from the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2093.htm#article3">I-II:93:3</a>; <a href="../summa/2095.htm#article2">I-II:95:2</a>). But <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> custom cannot change either the <a href="../cathen/09076a.htm">law of nature</a> or the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>. Therefore neither can it change <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, many <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evils</a> cannot make one <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>. But he who first acted against the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, did <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>. Therefore by multiplying such acts, nothing <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> is the result. Now a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is something <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>; since it is a rule of <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">human acts</a>. Therefore <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is not abolished by custom, so that the mere custom should obtain force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, the framing of laws belongs to those public men whose business it is to govern the community; wherefore private <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individuals</a> cannot make laws. But custom grows by the acts of private <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individuals</a>. Therefore custom cannot obtain force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, so as to abolish the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/02084a.htm">Augustine</a> says (Ep. ad Casulan. xxxvi): "The customs of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God's</a> people and the institutions of our ancestors are to be considered as laws. And those who throw contempt on the customs of the <a href="../cathen/03744a.htm">Church</a> ought to be punished as those who disobey the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> All <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> proceeds from the reason and will of the lawgiver; the Divine and <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> laws from the reasonable will of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>; the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> from the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a> of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, regulated by reason. Now just as <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a> and will, in practical matters, may be made manifest by speech, so may they be made <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> by <a href="../cathen/01115a.htm">deeds</a>: since seemingly a man chooses as <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> that which he carries into execution. But it is evident that by <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> speech, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> can be both changed and expounded, in so far as it manifests the interior movement and thought of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/12673b.htm">reason</a>. Wherefore by actions also, especially if they be repeated, so as to make a custom, <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> can be changed and expounded; and also something can be established which obtains force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in so far as by repeated external actions, the inward movement of the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a>, and concepts of reason are most effectually declared; for when a thing is done again and again, it seems to proceed from a deliberate judgment of reason. Accordingly, custom has the force of a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, abolishes <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, and is the interpreter of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> The <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> and Divine laws proceed from the Divine will, as stated above. Wherefore they cannot be changed by a custom proceeding from the <a href="../cathen/15624a.htm">will</a> of <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, but only by Divine authority. Hence it is that no custom can prevail over the Divine or <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> laws: for <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Synon. ii, 16): "Let custom yield to authority: <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a> customs should be eradicated by <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> and reason."</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> As stated above (<a href="../summa/2096.htm#article6">I-II:96:6</a>), <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws fail in some cases: wherefore it is possible sometimes to act beside the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>; namely, in a case where the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> fails; yet the act will not be <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>. And when such cases are multiplied, by reason of some change in <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>, then custom shows that the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is no longer useful: just as it might be declared by the verbal promulgation of a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to the contrary. If, however, the same reason remains, for which the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> was useful hitherto, then it is not the custom that prevails against the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, but the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that overcomes the custom: unless perhaps the sole reason for the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> seeming useless, be that it is not "possible according to the custom of the country" [<a href="../summa/2095.htm#article3">I-II:95:3</a>], which has been stated to be one of the <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>. For it is not easy to set aside the custom of a whole people.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> The people among whom a custom is introduced may be of two <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">conditions</a>. For if they are free, and able to make their own laws, the consent of the whole people expressed by a custom counts far more in favor of a particular observance, that does the authority of the sovereign, who has not the power to frame laws, except as representing the people. Wherefore although each <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a> cannot make laws, yet the whole people can. If however the people have not the free power to make their own laws, or to abolish a <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> made by a higher authority; nevertheless with such a people a prevailing custom obtains force of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in so far as it is tolerated by those to whom it belongs to make laws for that people: because by the very fact that they tolerate it they seem to approve of that which is introduced by custom.</p>

<h2 id="article4">Article 4. Whether the rulers of the people can dispense from human laws?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the rulers of the people cannot dispense from <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> laws. For the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> is established for the "common weal," as <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> says (Etym. v, 21). But the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> should not be set aside for the private convenience of an <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>: because, as the <a href="../cathen/01713a.htm">Philosopher</a> says (Ethic. i, 2), "the <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of the nation is more godlike than the <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> of one <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a>." Therefore it seems that a man should not be dispensed from acting in compliance with the general <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, those who are placed over others are commanded as follows (<a href="../bible/deu001.htm#verse17">Deuteronomy 1:17</a>): "You shall hear the little as well as the great; neither shall you respect any <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man's</a> <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">person</a>, because it is the judgment of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>." But to allow one <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> to do that which is equally forbidden to all, seems to be respect of <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a>. Therefore the rulers of a community cannot grant such dispensations, since this is against a precept of the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, in order to be <a href="../cathen/08571c.htm">just</a>, should accord with the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> and Divine laws: else it would not "foster religion," nor be "helpful to discipline," which is requisite to the <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a> of <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, as laid down by <a href="../cathen/08186a.htm">Isidore</a> (Etym. v, 3). But no <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> can dispense from the Divine and <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">natural</a> laws. Neither, therefore, can he dispense from the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> The <a href="../cathen/11567b.htm">Apostle</a> says (<a href="../bible/1co009.htm#verse17">1 Corinthians 9:17</a>): "A dispensation is committed to me."</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> Dispensation, properly speaking, denotes a measuring out to <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individuals</a> of some common goods: thus the head of a household is called a dispenser, because to each member of the household he distributes work and necessaries of life in due weight and measure. Accordingly in every community a man is said to dispense, from the very fact that he directs how some general precept is to be fulfilled by each <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>. Now it happens at times that a precept, which is conducive to the common weal as a general rule, is not <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> for a particular <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>, or in some particular case, either because it would hinder some greater <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>, or because it would be the occasion of some <a href="../cathen/05649a.htm">evil</a>, as explained above (<a href="../summa/2096.htm#article6">I-II:96:6</a>). But it would be dangerous to leave this to the discretion of each <a href="../cathen/07762a.htm">individual</a>, except perhaps by reason of an evident and sudden emergency, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2096.htm#article6">I-II:96:6</a>). Consequently he who is placed over a community is empowered to dispense in a <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> that rests upon his authority, so that, when the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> fails in its application to <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a> or circumstances, he may allow the precept of the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> not to be observed. If however he grant this permission without any such reason, and of his mere will, he will be an unfaithful or an imprudent dispenser: unfaithful, if he has not the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a> in view; imprudent, if he ignores the reasons for granting dispensations. Hence <a href="../cathen/08374c.htm">Our Lord</a> says (<a href="../bible/luk012.htm#verse42">Luke 12:42</a>): "Who, thinkest thou, is the faithful and wise dispenser [<a href="../cathen/05140a.htm">Douay</a>: steward], whom his lord setteth over his <a href="../cathen/05782a.htm">family</a>?"</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> When a <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">person</a> is dispensed from observing the general <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, this should not be done to the prejudice of, but with the <a href="../cathen/08069b.htm">intention</a> of benefiting, the common <a href="../cathen/06636b.htm">good</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> It is not respect of <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a> if unequal measures are served out to those who are themselves unequal. Wherefore when the <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">condition</a> of any <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">person</a> requires that he should reasonably receive special treatment, it is not respect of <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">persons</a> if he be the object of special favor.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> Natural <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, so far as it contains general precepts, which never fail, does not allow of dispensations. In other precepts, however, which are as conclusions of the general precepts, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> sometimes grants a <a href="../cathen/05041a.htm">dispensation</a>: for instance, that a loan should not be paid back to the betrayer of his country, or something similar. But to the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a> each <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> stands as a private <a href="../cathen/11726a.htm">person</a> to the public <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> to which he is subject. Wherefore just as none can dispense from public <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a>, except the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> from whom the <a href="../cathen/09053a.htm">law</a> derives its authority, or his delegate; so, in the precepts of the <a href="../cathen/09071a.htm">Divine law</a>, which are from <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, none can dispense but <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, or the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> to whom He may give special power for that purpose.</p>

<title>SUMMA THEOLOGIAE: Faith (Secunda Secundae Partis, Q. 1)</title><script src="https://dtyry4ejybx0.cloudfront.net/js/cmp/cleanmediacmp.js?ver=0104" async></script><script defer data-domain="newadvent.org" src="https://plausible.io/js/script.js"></script><link rel="canonical" href="https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3001.htm">

<meta name="description" content="Is the object of faith the First Truth? Is the object of faith something complex or incomplex, i.e. is it a thing or a proposition? <div id="mi5"><span class="breadcrumbs"><a href="../">Home</a> > <a href="../summa/">Summa Theologiae</a> > <a href="../summa/3.htm">Second Part of the Second Part</a> > Question 1</span></div>

<div id="springfield2">

<div class='catholicadnet-728x90' id='summa-728x90-top' style='display: flex; height: 100px; align-items: center; justify-content: center; '></div>

<h1>Question 1. Faith</h1>

<ol><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article1"> Is the object of faith the First Truth?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article2"> Is the object of faith something complex or incomplex, i.e. is it a thing or a proposition?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article3"> Can anything false come under faith?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article4"> Can the object of faith be anything seen?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article5"> Can it be anything known?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article6"> Should the things to be believed be divided into a certain number of articles?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article7"> These articles: are they of faith for all times?</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article8"> The number of articles</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article9"> The manner of embodying the articles in a symbol</a> </li><li><a href="../summa/3001.htm#article10"> Who has the right to propose a symbol of faith?</a> </li></ol>

<h2 id="article1">Article 1. Whether the object of faith is the First Truth?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not the First Truth. For it seems that the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is that which is proposed to us to be <a href="../cathen/02408b.htm">believed</a>. Now not only things pertaining to the Godhead, i.e. the First Truth, are proposed to us to be <a href="../cathen/02408b.htm">believed</a>, but also things concerning <a href="../cathen/08374c.htm">Christ's</a> <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, and the <a href="../cathen/13295a.htm">sacraments</a> of the <a href="../cathen/03744a.htm">Church</a>, and the <a href="../cathen/04211a.htm">condition</a> of creatures. Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not only the First Truth.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> and unbelief have the same object since they are opposed to one another. Now unbelief can be about all things contained in <a href="../bible/index.html">Holy Writ</a>, for whichever one of them a man denies, he is considered an unbeliever. Therefore <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> also is about all things contained in <a href="../bible/index.html">Holy Writ</a>. But there are many things therein, concerning <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> and other creatures. Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not only the First Truth, but also <a href="../cathen/04470a.htm">created</a> <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is condivided with <a href="../cathen/09397a.htm">charity</a>, as stated above (<a href="../summa/2062.htm#article3">I-II:62:3</a>). Now by <a href="../cathen/09397a.htm">charity</a> we love not only <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, who is the sovereign Good, but also our neighbor. Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">Faith</a> is not only the First Truth.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/05013a.htm">Dionysius</a> says (Div. Nom. vii) that "<a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is about the simple and everlasting <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a>." Now this is the First Truth. Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is the First Truth.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> The object of every cognitive <a href="../cathen/07099b.htm">habit</a> includes two things: first, that which is <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> materially, and is the material object, so to speak, and, secondly, that whereby it is <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a>, which is the formal aspect of the object. Thus in the science of geometry, the conclusions are what is <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> materially, while the formal aspect of the science is the mean of demonstration, through which the conclusions are <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a>.</p>

<p>Accordingly if we consider, in <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>, the formal aspect of the object, it is nothing else than the First Truth. For the <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> of which we are speaking, does not assent to anything, except because it is <a href="../cathen/13001a.htm">revealed</a> by <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>. Hence the mean on which <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is based is the Divine Truth. If, however, we consider materially the things to which <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> assents, they include not only <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, but also many other things, which, nevertheless, do not come under the assent of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>, except as bearing some relation to <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, in as much as, to wit, through certain effects of the Divine operation, <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">man</a> is helped on his journey towards the enjoyment of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>. Consequently from this point of view also the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is, in a way, the First Truth, in as much as nothing comes under <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> except in relation to <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, even as the object of the medical art is health, for it considers nothing save in relation to health.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> Things concerning <a href="../cathen/08374c.htm">Christ's</a> <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/10715a.htm">nature</a>, and the <a href="../cathen/13295a.htm">sacraments</a> of the <a href="../cathen/03744a.htm">Church</a>, or any creatures whatever, come under <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>, in so far as by them we are directed to <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, and in as much as we assent to them on account of the Divine Truth.</p>

<p>The same answer applies to the Second Objection, as regards all things contained in <a href="../bible/index.html">Holy Writ</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 3.</strong> <a href="../cathen/09397a.htm">Charity</a> also loves our neighbor on account of <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, so that its object, properly speaking, is <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a>, as we shall show further on (<a href="../summa/3025.htm#article1">II-II:25:1</a>.</p>

<h2 id="article2">Article 2. Whether the object of faith is something complex, by way of a proposition?</h2>

<p><strong>Objection 1.</strong> It would seem that the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not something complex by way of a proposition. For the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is the First Truth, as stated above (<a href="#article1">Article 1</a>). Now the First Truth is something simple. Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not something complex.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 2.</strong> Further, the exposition of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is contained in the symbol. Now the symbol does not contain propositions, but things: for it is not stated therein that <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> is almighty, but: "I <a href="../cathen/02408b.htm">believe</a> in <a href="../cathen/06608a.htm">God</a> .&nbsp;.&nbsp;. almighty." Therefore the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is not a proposition but a thing.</p>

<p><strong>Objection 3.</strong> Further, <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is succeeded by vision, according to <a href="../bible/1co013.htm#verse12">1 Corinthians 13:12</a>: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face. Now I <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">know</a> in part; but then I shall <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">know</a> even as I am <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a>." But the object of the heavenly vision is something simple, for it is the Divine Essence. Therefore the <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> of the wayfarer is also.</p>

<p><strong>On the contrary,</strong> <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">Faith</a> is a mean between science and opinion. Now the mean is in the same genus as the extremes. Since, then, science and opinion are about propositions, it seems that <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is likewise about propositions; so that its object is something complex.</p>

<p><strong>I answer that,</strong> The thing <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> is in the knower according to the mode of the knower. Now the mode proper to the <a href="../cathen/09580c.htm">human</a> <a href="../cathen/08066a.htm">intellect</a> is to <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">know</a> the <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a> by synthesis and analysis, as stated in <a href="../summa/1085.htm#article5">I:85:5</a>. Hence things that are simple in themselves, are <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">known</a> by the <a href="../cathen/08066a.htm">intellect</a> with a certain amount of complexity, just as on the other hand, the Divine <a href="../cathen/08066a.htm">intellect</a> <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knows</a>, without any complexity, things that are complex in themselves.</p>

<p>Accordingly the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> may be considered in two ways. First, as regards the thing itself which is <a href="../cathen/02408b.htm">believed</a>, and thus the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is something simple, namely the thing itself about which we have <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>. Secondly, on the part of the believer, and in this respect the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is something complex by way of a proposition.</p>

<p>Hence in the past both opinions have been held with a certain amount of <a href="../cathen/15073a.htm">truth</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 1.</strong> This argument considers the object of <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> on the part of the thing <a href="../cathen/02408b.htm">believed</a>.</p>

<p><strong>Reply to Objection 2.</strong> The symbol mentions the things about which <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a> is, in so far as the act of the believer is terminated in them, as is evident from the manner of speaking about them. Now the act of the believer does not terminate in a proposition, but in a thing. For as in science we do not form propositions, except in order to have <a href="../cathen/08673a.htm">knowledge</a> about things through their means, so is it in <a href="../cathen/05752c.htm">faith</a>.</p>
